chapter_theme: The first seventeen poems of Nalluruthiran's mullaikkali: six long songs of the herders' bull-catch (ஏறு கோள்), in which bulls coloured like the gods gore the young men in the pen, each feat is likened to an epic killing, and the herd girls, promised in advance to the man who takes a bull, sing in the kuravai that their shoulders are for no coward and praise the Pandya; then eleven dialogues of courtship among herd girls selling buttermilk and herders blocking their way, full of banter in the images of milking and churning, in which a chaplet falling into a girl's hair, a mother's silence or the town's gossip turns secret love into the kin's decision to marry.

comparisons.tenor: the glory lily putting out its swaying spathe like a drunk man's stance
the bulls' horns sharpened like the axe of the mighty god
the dun bull, coloured like the ulandu insect

comparisons.vehicle: நெஞ்சம் பிளந்து இட்டு, நேரார் நடுவண், தன் வஞ்சினம் வாய்த்தானும் போன்ம்
comparisons.tenor: the bull goring a herder, like the hero who split the chest of the man who seized a woman's hair and so kept his vow
the curled white mark on the black bull's forehead, like spreading flame
the black bull spilling a herder's entrails, like the god who tore the buffalo's chest and fed its entrails to the goblins
the white bull wrenching a herder, like the son who came in the night and twisted his father's killer

101.reading: When the first rains have budded the pidavam, the kodal and the kaya, the herders, crowned with those flowers, drive their sharp-horned bulls into the pen, pray at the ford, the banyan and the old maraa tree and leap in; three bulls gore their catchers, each like an epic killer (the one who tore open the chest of the man who seized a woman's hair, the god tearing the buffalo's chest at dusk, the son who twisted his father's killer in the night); the herd girls say the girl's shoulders go to the one who takes a bull that fears not even a rutting tusker, ask whether they should give their hair for pillow to those who sat aside, and say the boaster of the herd will be their man one day, until bulls and men are spent and the girls go with the herders into the mullai grove, every tryst kept.
101.nuance: The three goring scenes each end on an epic simile with போன்ம், so the village sport is told in the register of revenge and battle. Lines 39 to 42 are a taunt: the girls will not give their hair as pillow to the one who stood by with flute and staff while the bull gored others. The deity of lines 24 to 26 (பசும் கண் கடவுள், tearing the buffalo's chest and feeding the entrails to the goblins) is not named, and who is meant is not settled.

102.reading: A man watching the herd girls play in the rains, decked with pidavam, thalavam, thondri and konrai, asks who among them has today entered his life with her body, and is told she is the girl of whom it was cried before all that no one but the taker of a fighting bull may touch her; the festival is proclaimed, many men leap at the bulls and are thrown, then one herder appears clinging between neck and hump and wears his bull down; the speaker wonders that the herders' daughters, having seen a bull's neck broken yesterday, proclaim the bull-catch again today, and bids the drum keep up the kuravai while the hamlet's common rings with praise of the herder and the smiling girl.
102.nuance: The girl is promised in advance by public cry (எல்லாரும் கேட்ப அறைந்து), so the contest is a betrothal by ordeal rather than a sport. Lines 19 to 24 change metre into short clipped phrases (எழுந்தது துகள்; ஏற்றனர் மார்பு; கவிழ்ந்தன மருப்பு; கலங்கினர் பலர்) that enact the rush of the fight.

103.reading: Herders crowned with konrai, kaya, vetchi, pidavu, thalavu, kullai, kurunthu, kodal and paangar come to see the bull-catch while girls with teeth like jasmine buds throng the stand; bulls black with white feet, white with spots like the starred evening sky and red with horns curved like the crescent on the slayer's head fill a pen like a mountain cleft crowded with lion, horse, elephant and crocodile; they gore the herders until entrails wind round their horns like the god's crescent garland, and one herder drawing out entrails is like a man taking a red thread for the sacred triple thread; a girl points out to her friend herder after herder, one clinging to the hump like a garland, one riding like a boatman, one standing over the slain black bull so that her heart quaked as before Death tearing the buffalo's chest, one wrenching a red bull by the ear like Mayon splitting the horse's jaw; then men and girls dance the kuravai, and the girls say the herd girl will not embrace even in another birth the man who fears the horn, that her shoulders are not for the faint-hearted, and that herders' daughters ask no price but that a man fall between the killer bull's horns as between their breasts; the song ends with praise of the god and the king.
103.nuance: The girl's fear (என் நெஞ்சு உட்கிற்று, lines 45 and 55) is told twice through a god's terrible deed, so the herder she admires is seen as divine and dangerous at once. The closing lines put the terms of marriage in the girls' own mouths: no bride-price, only courage before the horn.

104.reading: The good herders of the ancient line that rose with the Pandya, who when the sea took his land went unwearied against enemy lands and set his fish emblem in place of the tiger and the bow, gather and pen bulls white like the palmyra-bannered god, black like the god with Sri on his chest, grey like the three-eyed one and red like the spear-bearer, massed like clouds; the girls are set on the stand like the moon ringed by stars, each promised to the taker of a named bull; a young black bull gores the man who leapt on the white bull's neck, like the dark god freeing the moon from the serpent, another bull rages with entrails on its horns like a killer elephant in smoke, a spotted bull turns away from a fallen man like a warrior who will not strike a foe who has lost his sword, and the pen is like the field where the five archers killed the hundred; after the kuravai a girl says she cannot rest without the chest of the man who broke the red-browed bull's pride though the cattle-folk talk, and the friend tells her that her kin have gladly agreed to give her to the herder who leapt on the black bull, trampling on the heads of the town that raised the gossip; the song ends with praise of the god of the discus and the Pandya.
104.nuance: The poem opens with Pandya history (the sea that swallowed his land, the Chola tiger and Chera bow displaced by the fish) and so ties the herders' festival to the dynasty. The spotted bull that spares a fallen man (lines 45 to 50) carries the battlefield rule of not striking the disarmed into the bull-pen. The bull-catch ends the gossip by producing the kin's consent.

105.reading: The herders of the old line gather to hold the god's guarding rite for the ancient drum-bearing house of the conqueror to whom the sea yielded pearls, and pen bulls whose marks are the gods' (black with a white curl like the conch at the discus-bearer's lips, white with a red spot like the garland of the one-earringed god, grey with a hump like the axe-bearer's dark throat, spotted like the thunderbolt-bearer's thousand eyes, red with white feet like the spear-bearer's white cloth), together like lion, axe, Kaalan and Death come to eat lives; the herders leap in amid thunderous drums and dust, the bulls hold them off, a red bull gores like Death, bells on another's horns are like bees round toddy buds, and the white bull carrying a man is like the moon slipping from the serpent's mouth; the herd girl's eyes cannot close looking at the face of the herder who took the bull, and she says to her friend: why did her kin rage like his bull because her hair smelled of mullai; what is it to those who cannot bear it, if her own kin bear what she has done with the herder's son; what joy equals this, that her mother beat her with a stick and the town made gossip linking her to the herder; and why give her now, when her heart went into the red bull's horns that day with him; the song ends with praise of the god on the serpent couch and the Pandya.
105.nuance: The girl counts her mother's beating and the town's gossip as joy, because they have made the bond public and so forced the marriage; her last lines date the real union to the moment the herder went between the horns. Each bull is coloured by a god's emblem, so the pen is a gathering of gods and of death at once (lines 20 to 22).

106.reading: Herders carrying their gear and sounding pots slung in nets, playing sweet flutes of konrai pod, come with their herds at the rainy hour to the wide wet field; the bulls, raising dust, pawing, bellowing and charging, are like warriors entering battle and, bloodied, like a line of rain clouds; the herders who part them into two groups are like the god who made the earth by parting the waves; the bulls gore them as if they were posts, yet the wounded herders do not rest but ride the bulls as fishermen ride their boats, and entrails dropped by kites hang on the branches like garlands on the banyan and kadamba; then the herd girls dance the kuravai holding the hands of the lovers who drove the bulls back, singing that they will bind the bull-gored wounds against their breasts, that the blood of the tamer on their curd-spotted shoulders is an ornament, that fear of the bull's head and desire for the herd girls' shoulders cannot go together, and asking whether their man will give them the wealth of hearing the town say 'her man took the killer bull' as they go selling buttermilk; they close by praising the forest and their warlike king.
106.nuance: The girls' song values the wound as the warrior poems value a wound taken facing the enemy, and asks for fame (the town's word) as the 'wealth' a husband brings. The fishermen's boats (line 24) bring a shore image into the herders' poem. Line 1, a list of the herders' gear, is obscure.

comparisons.tenor: the girl tying the fallen chaplet in her hair, like one who has found what she lost

107.reading: The girl tells her friend that when the cattle-herders penned their bulls as a challenge to the sheep-herders and others, the great spotted bull tossed with its horn the mullai chaplet from the head of the man who caught it by the ear and it fell into her hair, and she tied it up as if she had found something lost: will her mother hear? The friend asks what of it, it is his chaplet; the girl fears the mother will hear she tied a stranger's chaplet in her hair; the friend says all fault is cut away if he is a herder's son and she a herder's daughter and they love each other, if only her heart can become her mother's; the girl asks how she is to bear a sickness with no cure, and the friend tells her not to grieve: hearing that the bull put his chaplet in her washed hair, her father and brothers have all agreed that a great god has shown it, and have resolved to give her to that true herder.
107.nuance: The bull acts as the go-between: the kin read the chaplet falling into her hair as a god's sign (தெய்வ மால் காட்டிற்று), so chance becomes betrothal. The bull's act cannot be struck out without the poem's sense falling, so it is the subject, not iraicchi. Lines 1 to 4 (the challenge to the புல் இனத்தார் and the குடம் சுட்டவர்) are hard to construe.

108.reading: A herder meets a buttermilk girl and they trade words: he calls her the warrior who, wide in hips, shoulders and eyes and slender in brow, feet and waist, took up arms against his life, and asks how he wronged her; she mocks him as no herder, in his kaya chaplet and dark cloth leaning on his staff, but perhaps the sun-god's son; he says he will not argue with one who trusts her mullai-bud teeth, bamboo shoulders and battle eyes; she asks what she took from him that he stops her like a creditor; he says that by a stream rich in thalavam she ruled his heart as a battlefield with eyes like split young mangoes; she asks how she could rule his heart when her days go in taking food to her brother, pots to her father and the calves to graze; he urges her, since it is noon and the village near, to bathe in the rock pool, gather thalavam and mullai and stay with him in the kaya grove till dew falls; she tells him to keep such words for little herd girls, since like a bull that never tires of cows he goes after ten a day; he swears by the feet of the lord whose chest is like a mountain that none on earth surpasses her; and she, saying he will break that oath, sets the tryst: when the herders feast and dance the kuravai, unseen and unheard by his women, he is to call with the aambal flute, under the kaanchi tree in their garden.
108.nuance: The division of speakers is ours and several lines (20, 21, 49) are hard. The girl's mockery is courtship: she accuses him of many loves and then names the place, the signal and the hour of their meeting. The oath by the lord 'whose chest is joined with the hill' (மலையொடு மார்பு அமைந்த செல்வன்) names a god we cannot fix.

109.reading: A man tells a companion to look at the herd girl who comes with buttermilk, proud as the young heifer of an untiring fighting bull in a herd grazing the great grass of the rain-soaked field, as if she would raise gossip in big town and small: her beauty speaks to everyone, her eyes wound even the unwounded, her waist shows finer than her throat, as if the two beauties had given her all theirs, and Kama would lay down his arms if she entered the pen with the milk; the town's wives, agreeing she is fit to be an anangu to all, offer her mango pickle to send her away with her kin, guard their husbands and shut their doors all day when she comes.
109.nuance: The comedy is in the town's response: what the man sees as beauty the wives treat as a public danger and fence against. Lines 17 to 20 (the two beauties without waists, Kama laying down his weapons, the cattle-pen) are hard, and line 6 has a bracketed editorial letter.

comparisons.tenor: his life, yielding nothing, like milk churned for ghee that only wets the hand

110.reading: The herd girl tells the man that he goes after the good girls of every herder's house as if his desire were a cure for a scorpion sting, and takes her for easy, thinking a girl easy to buy buttermilk from is easy for butter too; he answers that his heart, as she shrinks back in fear and comes forward in weariness, circles her beauty like the rope round the churning stick, trembles daily like a heavy-bellied young cow that will not go home at dawn but circles her calf caught in the pen, and like milk churned for ghee yielding nothing, only wets the hand; she says he speaks so to every good woman he sees on the common, tells him to go before her kin see, and adds that tomorrow too she will go with the calves to the field.
110.nuance: Her last line, after the rebuff, tells him where she will be tomorrow, so the refusal carries an appointment. All his similes come from her own work of milking and churning, as if he speaks her trade back to her.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: a dialogue: the girl opens (lines 1 to 6) and closes (lines 20 to 23); the man speaks between

comparisons.tenor: the rebuffed herder walking away, like a man in distress

111.reading: The girl tells her friend that when she had tethered the calves after milking and gone in the blue-lily-bordered cloth her mother gave her to play with the herd girls where paangar and mullai spread, a herder in a kurunthu chaplet asked whether he might build her play-house, then tie a garland in her hair, then paint designs on her breasts, and she turned each offer back (he would sit in a house others built; a girl who took a stranger's flowers would be a great fool; should they wait for what others paint on them?), so that he went off as if stricken; and she asks the friend to tell her father and mother the ways of herd girls, so that the sickness she has caught may be cured.
111.nuance: The three refusals keep the herd girls' rule that a stranger's gifts are not taken, and her last sentence shows that she loves him: she wants him by the open road, through her parents. That is the friend's task of disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்), asked for in so many words.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the girl tells her friend of the herder's three offers and asks her to speak to her parents

comparisons.tenor: girls whose shoulders are like sugarcane that grew unplanted
the girl out at an hour when no one passes, as if herding calves

112.reading: Stopped on her way, the girl asks who this unlettered herder in a garland mixed with water lotus is, whom her kin told her to avoid and not speak to; he says his kin told him never to let go of girls with shoulders like unplanted sugarcane whose eyes bring love-sickness; she says his kin taught him well to stop good women and sing of their eyes and shoulders, and hers are skilled at watching; he says her kin would have slighted them if, while she herds calves at an hour when no one passes, those who know right ways did not speak to her; she says she knows, let go; he refuses: her kin forbade her to speak before him, not to embrace him, so let her embrace him gently and he will drink from her sharp teeth; and she reflects that if all the cunning herder said comes true they are joined, and if it proves false, then even should her eyes pale and her shoulders waste from his fragrant chest, it has its beauty.
112.nuance: The man turns her kin's prohibition into a loophole (they forbade speech, not embrace). Her last sentence accepts the risk of being deceived and counts even the pallor and wasting that would follow as beautiful. The speakers' turns are ours; lines 12 to 14 are hard to assign.

comparisons.tenor: the man blocking her path, like one gone mad

comparisons.vehicle: அரவு உற்று உருமின் அதிரும் குரல் போல்
comparisons.tenor: the bulls' bellowing, like the roar of thunder striking a serpent

iraicchi.act: the bulls stand together with their heifers, ready to go home with the herd
iraicchi.sense: as the bulls keep with their mates, the man means the two of them to go home together

113.reading: A man asks the girl with soft shoulders and restless eyes to tell him, before she goes, how he may escape the love-sickness she has caused; she asks who he is to stop her like a madman when they have never met; he says he is a son of the sheep-herders who fear no foe; she answers that, if so, her kin are the good cattle-herders of the pot-mark, there is no harm in talking but someone may come, so let her go; he will not let go on the word of one who consents and then withdraws, for how can he obey her word when his heart does not obey his; she asks why trust the lies of strangers; he says he is sure of her, and reminds her that they have often played with the companions in the cool sand groves of the forest stream, crowned with mullai and kurunthu: night has come, and the bulls roaring like thunder that strikes the serpent stand with the heifers, so that the herd may go home with them.
113.nuance: The two speak as members of rival herding groups (புல் இனத்து ஆயர், sheep and goats; குடம் சுட்டு நல் இனத்து ஆயர், cattle), and her objection is to his rank before it is to him. The closing image of the bulls standing with the heifers, ready to go home with the pair, is tagged as iraicchi below on a borderline deletion test.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: a dialogue: the man opens and closes; the girl answers in lines 4 to 5, 8 to 13 and 19 to 21

114.reading: The girl tells her friend, who laughed aloud when the kin began a wedding in her name with new flowers and called her a silly girl who knows nothing, to go to the herder and tell him, in words that will make him wonder, what she says: though the great wedding her kin prepare here, spreading sand low, washing the house with red earth and bringing a she-buffalo, be left void, she knows only the one wedding she made among her bright-browed companions who built play-houses on the striped sand of the ford; and even if they gained the whole sea-girt world, it is not the nature of herd girls of the hard way to join in two weddings.
114.nuance: She dates her marriage to the secret union, so a wedding to another man would be a second marriage that chastity forbids: karpu here precedes the kin's rite. The poem has two gaps (lines 2 and 18) and lines 1 to 2 (the crying son with long hair) do not fit the rest; much of the reading is uncertain. The she-buffalo of line 13 is a field-land animal in a herders' poem.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the girl sends her friend to the herder as the kin prepare a wedding with another; the occasion is the threat of a second marriage, which calls for the friend's disclosure

comparisons.vehicle: காணாமை உண்ட கடும் கள்ளை, மெய் கூர நாணாது சென்று நடுங்க உரைத்தாங்குக்
comparisons.tenor: their secret exposed, as those who drank strong toddy unseen then talk shamelessly till they shake
the mother shaking her hand, like one who has touched fire

115.reading: The girl tells her friend they have been caught red-handed, like those who drink strong toddy in secret and then go and talk shamelessly till they shake: she had tied in her hair a strand of mullai and the chaplet the herder wore, and when her mother had rubbed butter in and spread out her hair, the flower fell before her; the mother neither asked nor scolded but shook her hand like one who had touched fire and went out by the back door, and she, hair unbound, clutching her blue-lily cloth and faltering, hid in the paangar woods; the friend answers that there is nothing to fear: if she wore his chaplet, their people too have resolved to give her to him, will spread sand in the wide yard and hold the wedding here, and that is what they have planned every night.
115.nuance: The mother's silence (neither asking nor scolding) is the sharpest reproach in the poem and also its turning point: the flower makes the secret public, and the kin's decision follows. The kin's intention of line 18 (அடை சூழ்ந்தார்) is the same phrase as Kalittokai 107 line 33.

thurai_akam.note: the girl tells her friend how her mother found the flower; the friend answers (lines 17 to 21)

comparisons.tenor: the girl glaring at him, like a fierce young cow that charges those who come near

comparisons.vehicle: கன்று சேர்ந்தார்கண் கத ஈற்று ஆ சென்றாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the girl coming at him, as an angry new-calved cow goes at those near her calf
the man bowing his head and persisting, like a bull in heavy rain

116.reading: The girl tells the man who caught one end of her tether rope and stopped her as she went with the calves to the field to let her go; he refuses: she glares like a fierce young cow that charges those who come to touch it, and will rage when she leaves the pen-gate; she bids him keep off and not come at her like a cow that has calved going at those near its calf; he says let her mother come, or others, or even her king, he will not falter if she grants him grace; and she calls him shameless, one who ignores what she said, bows his head like a bull in heavy rain, answers back to everything and is lost in confusion, and who will seek out where she goes with the milk-pots and come even to the field.
116.nuance: Her last words (he will come even to the field where she takes the pots) tell him where to find her, so the scolding ends as an invitation. Both trade cattle images: the angry cow guarding her calf, the bull bowing under rain.

thurai_akam.note: a dialogue: the girl opens (lines 1 to 4) and closes (lines 13 to 17); the man speaks between; lines 8 and 9 may be his

comparisons.vehicle: மாண உருக்கிய நல் பொன் மணி உறீஇ, பேணித் துடைத்தன்ன மேனியாய்
comparisons.tenor: the girl's body, like refined gold set with gems and wiped clean
her breasts, like the unopened young buds of the kongu

117.reading: The man praises the girl, whose body is like refined gold set with gems and wiped clean and whose painted breasts are like the unopened buds of the kongu, and asks what she has in her hand; she says she is the daughter of the headman of the herders' quarter and it is a striped basket of palm strips that a pulaitti made for sale; he asks to be shown what is in it; she shows him the small mullai her friend picked with others by the forest; and he says that, if these are mullai and the hour is evening, now that he has seen her here he would tell her to go and let her go, but his understanding, not weighing it, is too weak.
117.nuance: The mullai flowers, the flower of evening and of waiting, turn his small talk into a claim: the hour of meeting has come, and he cannot let her go. She names her father's rank before anything else.

links.note: Kalittokai 101 says the herd girl's shoulders go to the one who seizes a bull that does not fear even a rutting tusker (கடாஅக் களிற்றினும் கண்ணஞ்சா ஏற்றை); Purananuru 342 says the chieftain's daughter's beauty is for fighters alone (பொருநர்க்கு அல்லது பிறர்க்கு ஆகாதே), her brothers threshing the battlefield with elephants for oxen.
links.teaches: Both give the girl only to proven courage, but the chieftain's family proves it in a war that uses elephants as threshing oxen, while the herders stage the proof on their own working animal inside a fenced pen, so the mullai contest is the puram bride-test turned from a siege that ruins the town into a bounded festival.

links.note: Purananuru 343: the father refuses even wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri humbly offered, and suitors' armies crowd the town; Kalittokai 103: the herd girls say they want no price (விலை வேண்டார்), only a man who will fall between the killer bull's horns as between their breasts.
links.teaches: Read together they show who sets the bride's terms: in the puram town the father refuses wealth and the girl becomes the cause of a war, while in the herders' song the girls voice the refusal themselves and name the one price they accept, so the mullai poem gives the woman the choice the puram poem leaves to her father and the kings.

links.note: Kalittokai 104 likens the pen strewn with gored men to the field where the five archers killed the hundred (நூற்றுவர் மடங்க... ஐவர் அட்ட பொரு களம்); Purananuru 2 praises the Chera who gave food without limit while the hundred fought the five and fell on the field.
links.teaches: The Bharata war that Purananuru 2 treats as a dated occasion for one king's generosity is already, in Kalittokai, a stock picture of any heap of the fallen, used even for a village bull-catch, so the epic had passed from a remembered event into the common image store of the poets.

links.note: Kural 1150: the friend says the town raises the very gossip they want, and the lover will grant marriage if asked; Kalittokai 104: the friend tells the girl that her kin have gladly agreed to give her to the herder who leapt on the black bull, trampling on the heads of the town that raised the gossip (அலர் எடுத்த ஊராரை உச்சி மிதித்து).
links.teaches: The couplet hopes that the town's talk will move the lover to marry; the herders' poem shows a second way gossip ends, through the kin's public consent once the bull is taken, so in the mullai village it is the girl's family the gossip moves, and the wedding then silences the town.

links.note: Kural 1147: the sickness of love grows long with the town's gossip for manure and the mother's words for water; Kalittokai 105: the girl asks what joy equals this, that her mother beat her with a stick and the town made gossip linking her to the herder (யாய் என்னைக் கண் உடைக் கோலள் அலைத்ததற்கு... அலர் செய்துவிட்டது இவ் ஊர்).
links.teaches: The same two forces, the town's talk and the mother's harshness, feed a growing pain in the couplet but are welcomed as joy by the herd girl, because once the bond is public her marriage follows from the bull-catch; whether exposure hurts depends on whether an open road to marriage lies ahead.

links.note: Purananuru 278: the old mother, told her son fled, searches the field and rejoices more than at his birth to find him cut to pieces; Kalittokai 106: the herd girls sing that they will bind the bull-gored wounds against their breasts and that the tamer's blood on their curd-spotted shoulders is an ornament.
links.teaches: Akam takes over the puram pride in wounds taken facing the foe and moves it from the mother to the beloved: the wound that proves in Purananuru 278 that a son died well proves in Kalittokai 106 that a man is fit to be embraced, so the herd girls' desire is built on the warrior ethic.

links.note: In Kalittokai 107 the bull tosses the herder's mullai chaplet into the girl's hair by chance; in 115 she herself tied his chaplet in her hair and it fell before her mother; in both the kin then resolve to give her to him (அடை சூழ்ந்தார்).
links.teaches: The same outcome from accident in one poem and from the girl's own act in the other shows that among the herders the man's flowers in a girl's hair bind her however they got there: the kin read the first as a god's sign and the second as a fact to be ratified, and both end in betrothal.

links.note: Kural 1083: the man says he now knows Death, which has a woman's grace and big eyes that make war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு); Kalittokai 108: the man calls the girl the warrior who took up arms against his life, and mocks her trust in her mullai-bud teeth and battle eyes (பேர் அமர் உண் கண்ணும்), while she answers back and at last sets the tryst.
links.teaches: The couplet's lone confession of being slain by her eyes appears in the herders' poem as a line of banter that the girl hears, throws back and answers with a meeting place, which shows the conceit of the killing eye at work as courtship speech addressed to the woman, not only as the man's inner wonder.

links.note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Kalittokai 109: the man watching the buttermilk girl reports that the town's wives, judging her fit to be an anangu to everyone (யார்க்கும் அணங்கு ஆதல் சான்றாள்), keep their husbands in and shut their doors when she comes.
links.teaches: Beside the couplet, the herders' poem shows that the word அணங்கு named a real danger, a beauty that strikes whoever sees it: what is one man's private bewilderment in the Kural becomes in Kalittokai a judgment the whole town shares and acts on by guarding its men.

links.note: Akananuru 180: while the girls play at sand houses, a man drives up, hangs a kuvalai wreath down her braid unasked, gazes and leaves, and the town starts talking; Kalittokai 111: a herder offers to build the girl's play-house, tie a garland in her hair and paint her breasts, and she refuses each, saying a girl who takes a stranger's flowers is a great fool (ஏதிலார் தந்த பூக் கொள்வாய்).
links.teaches: The herd girl's refusal states the rule the shore poem leaves unsaid, that a stranger's flowers in a girl's hair are a claim on her; that rule is why the silent wreath of Akananuru 180 sets the town talking, and why the herd girl answers the same offer by asking her friend to tell her parents.

links.note: Akananuru 86 presents the rite (sand spread under the pandal, தருமணல் ஞெமிரி; the matrons' blessing of chastity; the kin giving the bride, தமர்தர) as the start of the marriage; in Kalittokai 114 the girl, seeing her kin prepare a wedding with sand spread low (தரு மணல் தாழப் பெய்து), says she knows only the one union she made among her play-house companions and that two weddings are against the nature of herd girls. On this reading the rite that makes a marriage in 86 makes none in 114.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that akam could place the binding moment of marriage either in the kin's sand-strewn rite or before it in the secret union, so the same ceremony that founds a wife's chastity in Akananuru 86 would, given to another man, be a forbidden second marriage for the herd girl.
